2. The game

2.1 Theme

Agawang Base is a Filipino street game of two bases and two teams. One team defends its base while the other tries to steal a member — or, in this adaptation, a flag — and the tension comes from the moment you leave your own base undefended. Agawan Base 3D keeps that structure and makes it playable on a phone in landscape, with a short 180-second match that fits a class break.

The theme is not a skin. The mechanics that make the street game recognisable are the mechanics the code implements: a base you can be tagged near, a prisoner you can free, a flag that decides the match, and short immunity after a rescue so a freed player is not tagged again instantly.

2.2 Target player and what that decided

The target player is someone who played agawan base as a child and now has a mid-range Android phone and ten minutes. That single sentence drove concrete decisions:

  • Landscape, two thumbs. Controls sit at the bottom corners, and every button is at least 144 canvas px (≈ 48 dp) tall, so the controls are reachable while gripping a phone in two hands.
  • 30 fps target, not 60. A steady 30 suits a top-down chase game and roughly halves the thermal cost on a mid-range phone. The profile in §8 is measured against a 33.3 ms budget.
  • The rules teach themselves. The HOW TO PLAY screen exists because the game does not assume the player knows the house rules; it explains tagging, rescuing and the flag in the same words the code uses.

2.3 Core loop

Landscape top-down chase: move with the on-screen stick, tag opponents, free your teammates, steal the red flag and carry it home while your own base holds. A match is won by eliminating the opposing team or by capturing the flag. Difficulty is Easy, Normal or Hard, applied identically to both teams so the setting changes how demanding the match is rather than quietly handicapping the player's side.

2.4 The rules, as implemented

These are the constants in code, not design intentions:

Rule Value Where
Tag reach 1.2 m MatchManager.cs:88
Flag steal reach 1.5 m MatchManager.cs:91
Rescue reach 1.5 m MatchManager.cs:110
Immunity after rescue 2 s MatchManager.cs:119
Rescue cooldown 3 s MatchManager.cs:123
Match time limit 180 s (0 disables) MatchManager.cs:128
Dropped flag auto-returns 10 s Flag.cs:44
Team sizes 1v1 to 4v4 MatchSettings

The two safeguards that keep a match from stalling or looping are worth naming: a just-freed player ignores rescuers for the cooldown (MatchManager.cs:416), which stops endless chain-rescues, and a dropped flag returns itself after ten seconds (Flag.cs:181), which stops a match becoming a standoff over a flag nobody can reach.

5. Architecture at a glance

Five folders under Assets/Scripts/, compiled into three assemblies — AgawanBase.Runtime, AgawanBase.Editor, AgawanBase.Tests.EditMode:

  • Core — the data and rules primitives: MatchSettings, MapDefinition, Team, TeamManager, PlayerProfile, CharacterStatus, CharacterMotor, SprintStamina, GameFeedback, ReleaseInfo.
  • Gameplay — MatchManager (the referee), EnemyAI split into .Perception, .Scoring and .Actions partials, Flag, HideSpot, PlayerController, CharacterSpawner, MapNavigator.
  • UI — GameManager (the screen state machine), HudController, MapSelectUI, MatchSetupUI, ProfileUI, OffScreenMarkers, VirtualJoystick, SafeAreaFitter, SprintButton.
  • Visual — presentation that must not own rules: CharacterBars, IndicatorController, CharacterBushHide, CharacterFacing, CharacterRigAnimator, FollowCamera.
  • Diagnostics — PerfCapture, PerfScenario.

The separation that matters most in a defense is that Visual reads rules and never writes them. IndicatorController.cs:24 states the contract in a tooltip, and it exists because a presentation layer that mutates match state is how a "won" match ends up disagreeing with the HUD.

The full diagram is Docs/Zedrich Abrera/Week_17/Evidence/architecture.svg, and the consolidated technical account is the companion Abrera_Zedrich_PA2_Technical_Report.pdf.

6. Security and player data

The one piece of player data the game holds is the profile. It is stored as a file, not PlayerPrefs, precisely so it can carry an integrity signature (PlayerProfile.cs:80–95): a SHA-256 over a per-install random salt followed by the payload JSON.

What it does: a profile edited by hand no longer matches its signature, so it is rejected and set aside as profile.rejected.json instead of being trusted (PlayerProfile.cs:537–540).

What it does not do: it cannot stop a determined attacker who controls the device, because the salt is on that same device and there is no server to verify against. The source says so in its own comment rather than overclaiming, and this document repeats it.

That limit was observed working in an unplanned place: the Windows backup package, sharing a persistent data path with the editor, found an editor-written profile, could not verify it, refused it and preserved it. That is recorded in Evidence/windows_backup_build.md §5 — a real rejection, not a hypothetical one.

Secret handling is recorded in Week_17/Evidence/secret_scan.md, with the raw scan output kept beside it.

8. Optimisation

Week 16 profiled the shipping path and made one change worth naming: prop texture memory fell from 21,849 KB to 1,369 KB, a reduction of 20.0 MB, by removing texture memory the low-poly art was not using. The measured frame cost afterwards was a main thread of 0.59–0.63 ms and a GPU time of 0.48 ms across 17 render events, with about 320 bytes allocated per frame, against a 33.3 ms budget at render scale 0.80.

One point of honesty that the technical report repeats: the Week 16 → Week 17 download shrank from 68.30 MB to 31.63 MB because the build changed from development to release. That is not claimed as an optimisation. Nothing was removed from the game; debug symbols and development checks were.

9. The Windows backup package

Abrera_Zedrich_PA2_Windows.zip (39.39 MB, MD5 fe17f2060c994218e4593b2010eb9a98) is a compiled Windows player built from the same tree, provided because no Android handset is attached to the machine that produced this submission (adb devices is empty). It was launched and confirmed to reach the title screen, printing the same 1.0.0-rc1 - built 2026-11-19 string as the APK.

It is a backup, and it differs from the submission in three disclosed ways: it runs Mono rather than IL2CPP, it has no haptics (GameFeedback.cs:174 guards the catch buzz behind UNITY_ANDROID || UNITY_IOS), and two post-processing passes — Gaussian/Bokeh depth of field and Panini projection — are stripped from the Standalone build. Detail and the player log excerpt are in Evidence/windows_backup_build.md §6.

A backup that is quietly different from the submission is worse than none, so the differences are listed rather than glossed.

10. Limitations and honest gaps

Written down because the module asks for limitations and because the alternative is a document that claims more than the evidence supports.

  1. The APK was not installed on a handset for this submission. No device is available. The submitted file is hashed and unmodified, but "it installs and runs on a phone" is not something this Week 18 submission demonstrates. It is marked BLOCKED, not passed.
  2. The repository was local-only until 2026-11-19. origin/main sat at d08fc9b, which predates Weeks 15–17, so at the time of writing the instructor could not verify the final tag or commit from the remote. It has since been published: origin/main is 5e63b1c and v1.0.0-pa2, v1.0.0-rc1 and week16-final all resolve remotely. Evidence/repo_state.txt keeps the pre-push state as a record.
  3. E3 is sat under supervision and had not been sat when this document was written. Evidence/e3_record.md is a record with fields, and Evidence/defense_prep.md holds pointers to files and commits, never scripted answers.
  4. Two Week 14 discoverability findings were never re-tested against the rebuilt instructions screen.
  5. AI balance rests on 16 regression scenarios, not on a large-scale study.
  6. The Windows backup has not been playtested on a desktop. The Week 14 usability data applies to the handset APK, not to this package.
